script.title: Operating Cycle: Gross and Net
script.caption_hook: How long is your cash stuck in the business? The operating cycle explains it.

lines.say: Ma'am, how long is our cash stuck in a business?
Imagine a factory buying raw material, making goods, selling on credit and finally collecting cash.
So that whole journey takes time?
It starts when cash is spent on raw material, moves through work in progress, finished goods and debtors, until cash comes back.
Yes. Gross cycle is R plus W plus F plus D, each in days.
But suppliers give us credit too, right?
Exactly. We deduct the creditors period C, because supplier credit postpones our cash going out. That gives the net cycle.

board.title: Net cycle
board.formula: O = R + W + F + D − C
board.sub: O = net days; C = creditors period

lines.say: Say R is 30 days, W 10, F 20, D 40 and C 30. Gross is 100 days.
Yes, 70 days. If cost per day is ₹1,000, working capital needed is ₹70,000.
So a longer net cycle needs more working capital?
Yes. Remember: net cycle equals R plus W plus F plus D minus C. Supplier credit shortens it.

check_notes: Writer: Worked example: R 30 + W 10 + F 20 + D 40 = 100 gross days; minus C 30 = 70 net days; 70 x ₹1,000 cost per day = ₹70,000. Line 4 shortened slightly to fit the 22-word limit while keeping the examiner's sequence.

Checker: Line 12 (voice and board): 'cost per day' doesn't say what cost or over what period, so it's ambiguous (purchase cost? sales value?). Suggested wording: 'If total operating cost is ₹1,000 per day (annual operating cost ÷ 360), working capital needed is ₹1,000 × 70 days = ₹70,000.' Add a board label such as 'Operating cost/day'. It is also worth saying this is a simplified estimate: it uses one cost rate for every stage and leaves out any minimum cash balance.
